title: Method
text:
Cases. Buildings HPD ordered vacated for fire damage (pilot: January 2025).
Comparison buildings. Residential buildings on the same block, of similar size (from about a third to three times as many apartments), built before 2000. Same-block matching holds neighborhood, era and building stock roughly constant.
Records before the event only. Every count uses records dated before the cutoff (pilot: January 1, 2025). The full study adds a 60-day gap before each fire.
Rank within the block. Each case’s value is ranked against its own neighbors (0% = lowest on the block, 100% = highest, ties split).
Test against chance. A permutation test repeatedly picks a random building on each block as a fake “case.” The p-value is the share of 20,000 shuffles whose average rank is as high as the real cases’.

title: Method
text:
Known biases

Inspection intensity. Violations exist only where someone inspected, and inspections follow tenant complaints. A building with organized tenants can look worse than a neglected building whose tenants don’t call.
Coverage. HPD covers rental housing; one- and two-family owner-occupied homes rarely appear.
Timing. Violations written right after a fire can look like warnings unless records near the event are excluded.
Small samples. The pilot has 7 fire cases and 9 collapse cases.

title: Method
text:
Full-study plan
Conditional logistic regression on matched sets (the standard model for this design), a machine-learning pass (LightGBM with SHAP explanations) to find combinations, and a temporal holdout: fit on 2018–2023 fires, then test how well the signals rank 2024–2025 fires.

title: Can public records flag NYC buildings at risk of fire?
text:
In a pilot of 7 NYC buildings vacated after fires, their HPD “immediately hazardous” (Class C) violations per apartment ranked on average at the 87th percentile of comparable buildings on their own block, using only records from before the fire.
New York publishes millions of housing and building records: every HPD code violation, DOB complaint, stop-work order and permit. This project asks whether those records, read together, can identify buildings at higher risk of a serious fire before it happens, and which patterns of owner neglect carry the signal.

A risk signal is a reason to look more closely at a building, not proof that an owner caused a fire. This site publishes patterns, not lists of individual buildings or landlords.

title: Case study: 2625 Bedford Avenue
text:
On November 11, 2026, the three-story building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue in Brooklyn partially collapsed, and at least one person died. It stood next to a construction site at 2625 Bedford Avenue, where a one-story building had been demolished. A DOB violation issued that day attributes the collapse to “unsafe construction at 2625 Bedford Ave.”
The public record shows warning signs at the construction site, not at the building that fell.

title: Case study: 2625 Bedford Avenue
text:
The building that collapsed
1321 Flatbush Avenue (four apartments, built 1930) had a long list of HPD violations the owner never corrected, including Class C violations from August 2024 for sprinkler water supply, self-closing doors and exposed wiring, and a leaking roof cited in 2022, 2024 and 2026. None described cracks, bulging or settlement. Its only DOB violations before the collapse were from 2019, for an advertising sign. No DOB complaints had been filed about it.

title: Case study: 2625 Bedford Avenue
text:
What this case suggests
The strongest signal sat on the adjacent lot: a complaint about work beyond its permits, a stop-work order that was ignored, then a contractor change, all next to an old masonry building in poor repair. That points to a test the building-by-building approach misses: construction negligence on a neighboring lot, weighted by the condition of the buildings around it.

Investigators had not determined the cause at the time of writing. This page reports what public records show; it does not assign fault. Records from NYC Open Data: DOB Violations (3h2n-5cm9), ECB Violations (6bgk-3dad), DOB Complaints (eabe-havv), DOB NOW Permits (rbx6-tga4), HPD Violations (wvxf-dwi5).

text: Of the 7 buildings in the pilot, 4 had the highest rate of Class C (“immediately hazardous”) HPD violations per apartment among comparable buildings on their block. DOB records alone did not set them apart.

title: Fire findings (pilot)
section: What it means, and what it doesn’t
text:
What it means, and what it doesn’t

The signal is HPD-specific. For fires, conditions tenants report to HPD (wiring, detectors, doors, heat, general disrepair) carry the signal. In a matching pilot on structural collapses, the pattern reversed: DOB history mattered and HPD alone did not.
Seven cases is a lead, not a finding. The full study scales this to every HPD fire-damage vacate since 2018, with matched controls and a held-out test on later fires.
Some violations may follow the fire. If a fire happened in late 2024 and the vacate order came in January 2025, post-fire inspections could count as “warnings.” The full study only uses records from at least 60 days before each fire.
More complaints mean more inspections. Buildings with active tenants generate more violations. The full study controls for complaint volume.


Method: how the comparison works. Code: pilot/fire_analyze.py and pilot/pilot_stats.py.

title: Data & code
text:
About the pilot data
The pilot used the Open Data API’s server-side aggregation (counts by lot and violation class) one block at a time. Those counts are saved in pilot/fire_data.py and pilot/collapse_data.py, so the pilot can be checked without downloading anything. The full pipeline rebuilds them from the raw datasets.
